supports.prints: May be harmful if swallowed or inhaled (H303+H333)
supports.where: Section 2, the one hazard class it lists: category 5, for acute toxicity by mouth and by breathing in, one statement under a pair of codes. The note gives the codes and says the statement in the project's words. The section prints no other hazard code, no precautionary statement and no other sentence.

Section 3, the concentration column, in the row for barium chloride, which the formula column gives as the dihydrate, formula weight 244.28; the rest is water. The sheet does not say on what basis the percentage is. Counted as the dihydrate, 0.1 mol/L is about 24 g in a litre, about 2.4 g in each 100 mL (worked out, not read here), a shade under the foot of this range. The title's range takes the solution in, and a solution a little under the table's range is not one the sheet would rate higher. The note's 2% counts the salt without its water: about 21 g in a litre.

Section 11, the first words after the label for acute effects; the line for target organs in the same section starts with the heart, the nerves and the kidneys and goes on to four more. Section 2 of the sheet rates its solution in category 5 all the same. The note gives both, so that the one statement is not read as the whole of what the sheet says.
The heading of section 8. Under it the sheet calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing, and for washing the hands after handling; it prints no code beside either.

The heading of section 4. Under it, for the eyes: they are rinsed with water for several minutes, contact lenses are taken out if they are worn and come out easily, and the rinsing is kept up after that; the sheet prints no code beside this and gives no number of minutes. For the skin: it is washed with plenty of water. For swallowing: the mouth is rinsed and a poison centre or a doctor is called if the person feels unwell; the section's first line says the same of any exposure, with the code P312.

The heading of section 13. Under it the sheet has two lines: that the federal, state and local rules that may apply are to be looked at first, and that one of the supplier's own numbered methods (#27h) is one option. The note gives no method of disposal, this one or another. Section 12, on ecology, has one line, that there is no data yet. Section 6 says that a spill is held with sand or an absorbent and put into a closed bag or container. None of the three says anything of drains, of waterways or of the environment. Section 15 prints RCRA D005 among its listings; the note does not give the code.

The same supplier's sheet for a 0.2 M solution (SDS No. BB0037, revised June 14, 2024), read the same day at https://digitalassets.avantorsciences.com/adaptivemedia/rendition/id_812a8bebfed5fa00a3355f52c7279e6f00fba879/vid_812a8bebfed5fa00a3355f52c7279e6f00fba879/prid_original/clid_SAPDAM, prints the same signal word, the same two classes and statements, the same precautionary statements, the same first aid and the same lines on spills and disposal as this one; it is not a source of the record.
Section 2, after the words Signal word. The sheet prints it in capitals; the note gives it as Warning.

Section 2, the first of the two hazard statements; the class beside it is acute toxicity by mouth, category 4. The first supplier's sheet for its solution has category 5 for the same route, with H303. The note gives the code and says that this is the graver.

supports.prints: H333: May be harmful if inhaled.
supports.where: Section 2, the second of the two hazard statements; the class beside it is acute toxicity by breathing in, category 5, as in the first supplier's sheet. The section prints no other hazard statement, and none for the eyes or the skin.
Section 3, in the row for barium chloride dihydrate; water is the rest, at 97.56%. It is the figure 0.1 mol/L comes to when the salt is counted as the dihydrate.

Section 2, the first of the precautionary statements. The others are P264, on washing the hands; P270, that nobody eats, drinks or smokes while using the product; P301+P330+P312 and P304+P312, on calling a poison centre or a doctor after swallowing or breathing it in; and P501, on disposal. Section 8 says that safety glasses, goggles or a face shield, a laboratory coat or apron and gloves are to be worn, and that an eyewash and a safety shower are to be at hand.

The heading of section 4. Under it, for the eyes: contact lenses are looked for and taken out, the eyes are flushed with water for 15 minutes or more, the upper and lower lids lifted from time to time, and medical attention is got at once. For the skin: contaminated clothing is taken off and the skin flushed with mild soap and water, with medical attention if it becomes irritated. For swallowing: a doctor or a poison centre is called at once, and vomiting is brought on only if medical staff say so.

The heading of section 6. Under it, as an environmental precaution: runoff is to be kept from storm sewers and from ditches that lead to waterways. A spill is taken up with a dry inert material and put into a container for disposal, and the place washed. Section 13 says that its guidance is for small amounts, and that disposal is to follow the local, state and federal rules or go through a licensed agency for chemical disposal. Section 12 ends with a line that harm to the environment cannot be ruled out if the product is handled or disposed of carelessly. The note says the first of these in its own words and gives no method of disposal. Section 15 lists the code D005 for barium chloride in its column for RCRA; the note does not give the code.
